title: Sample Spaces and Events
intro: A probability model starts with a sample space, the set of all possible outcomes. Events are subsets of it, so the logic of events is the algebra of sets.

blocks.text: An experiment is anything with an uncertain result: rolling two dice, measuring a lifetime, recording tomorrow's weather. The sample space $\Omega$ is the set of all possible outcomes, chosen fine enough that exactly one outcome occurs. For two dice the natural choice is the 36 ordered pairs $(i, j)$; recording only the sum would lose information you might need later, such as whether a double was rolled.
An event is a subset $A\subseteq\Omega$: the event occurs when the outcome lies in $A$. The logical operations become set operations:

items: 'A and B': the intersection $A\cap B$, often written $AB$.
'A and B cannot both happen': $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, $A\cap B = \emptyset$.
De Morgan's laws: $(A\cup B)^c = A^c\cap B^c$ and $(A\cap B)^c = A^c\cup B^c$. 'Not (A or B)' means 'neither'.

blocks.text: When $\Omega$ is finite and symmetry makes every outcome equally likely, probability is counting:

blocks.caption: The classical definition. It only applies when the outcomes really are equally likely.

blocks.text: The two-dice example: the sum is 7 for 6 of the 36 pairs, so $P(\text{sum} = 7) = 1/6$. At least one six occurs in 11 pairs (six with a six first, six with a six second, minus the double six counted twice). Counting larger sets is the subject of Counting (#/probability/foundations/counting).
Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts the outcomes in both twice, so

blocks.tex: P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)
blocks.caption: The two-event case of inclusion–exclusion.

blocks.text: and the complement rule $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ is often the fastest route: 'at least one' is usually easiest as one minus 'none'.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from itertools import product
# The sample space of two fair dice: 36 equally likely ordered pairs.
omega = list(product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
P = lambda event: sum(1 for w in omega if event(w)) / len(omega)
A = lambda w: w[0] + w[1] == 7          # the sum is 7
B = lambda w: w[0] == 6 or w[1] == 6    # at least one six
print(f"P(A) = {P(A):.4f}  (6/36)")
print(f"P(B) = {P(B):.4f}  (11/36)")
print(f"P(A and B) = {P(lambda w: A(w) and B(w)):.4f}  (2/36)")
print(f"P(A or B) = {P(lambda w: A(w) or B(w)):.4f} = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = {P(A) + P(B) - P(lambda w: A(w) and B(w)):.4f}")
# The same probabilities by simulation: relative frequencies settle on them
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(100000, 2))
print("simulated P(A) =", np.mean(rolls.sum(1) == 7), " simulated P(B) =", np.mean((rolls == 6).any(1)))

blocks.text: Output of the run: $P(A) = 0.1667$, $P(B) = 0.3056$, $P(A\cap B) = 0.0556$, and both ways of computing $P(A\cup B)$ give 0.4167. Over 100 000 simulated rolls the relative frequencies are 0.168 and 0.305: frequencies settle on probabilities, a fact made precise by The Law of Large Numbers (#/probability/limit-theorems/law-of-large-numbers).

blocks.title: Three coins
blocks.text: Three fair coins are tossed. Write the sample space and find the probability of at least two heads.
solution: $\Omega$ has $2^3 = 8$ equally likely outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT.
At least two heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, which is 4 outcomes, so the probability is $4/8 = 1/2$.

blocks.title: Union from the parts
blocks.text: $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A\cap B) = 0.2$. Find $P(A\cup B)$ and the probability that neither occurs.
solution: Neither is the complement of the union (De Morgan): $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$.

blocks.title: At least one six
blocks.text: What is the probability of at least one six in four rolls of a fair die?
solution: The complement is 'no six in four rolls': $(5/6)^4 = 625/1296 \approx 0.482$.
So $P(\text{at least one six}) = 1 - 0.482 = 0.518$, a little better than even. (This is de Méré's old wager.)
